feedback: When a rhombus is placed and only the sides indicator is green: 'All four sides are equal — but look at the angles indicator. Two angles are acute, two obtuse, so the angles are NOT all equal. Failing either condition makes it irregular.'

When a non-square rectangle is placed: 'All four angles are equal right angles — but the sides are not all the same length, so it is still irregular. It mirrors the rhombus, which fails on the other condition.'
When the square passes both: 'Both equal sides AND equal angles — this is the one quadrilateral that turns both keys, so it is regular.'
If a child predicts the rhombus is regular: 'That uses only the sides. Run the angle check too before deciding.'
activities.intendedInsight: Regularity is a conjunction: equal sides alone, or equal angles alone, is not enough — the badge is a two-key lock, and only a shape that turns both keys (the square among quadrilaterals) is regular.
learnerActions: Work with an adjustable polygon (3–8 sides) that can be reshaped, with two visible condition indicators overhead — 'all sides equal' and 'all angles equal' — and a 'REGULAR' badge that lights only when BOTH indicators are green.
Start with a square: confirm both indicators are green and the badge reads REGULAR.

Skew the square so it leans into a rhombus — the tool keeps all four sides equal — and watch the sides stay equal (green) while the angles become unequal (red), so the badge drops to IRREGULAR even though every side is still the same length.

Straighten the rhombus back into a square, then stretch it along one direction into a long rectangle: watch the angles stay as four right angles (green) while the sides are no longer all equal (red) — still IRREGULAR.

Take named shapes from a gallery (rhombus, oblong rectangle, square, regular pentagon, irregular pentagon) and place each onto the checker, predicting first whether it will be regular and which condition (if any) it fails.
Attempt a 'make it regular' challenge that only succeeds when both conditions hold at once.
activities.title: The two-key lock: checking both conditions on a changing shape

feedback: If a shape is sorted by look: 'Decide with the two columns, not how neat it looks — a tilted regular pentagon is still regular, and a neat oblong rectangle is still irregular.'
If the rhombus is placed with the regular group: 'Check the angle column. Sides tick, angles cross — it belongs with the irregular shapes.'
Confirm correct discrimination: 'You separated the rhombus (sides only) from the rectangle (angles only) from the square (both) — exactly the three cases that break the single-criterion habit.'
activities.intendedInsight: Classifying by explicitly checking both conditions — not by overall appearance or by sides alone — and recognising that 'regular' is not welded to a symmetric-looking prototype.
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set of polygons into 'regular' and 'irregular' groups, including many-sided shapes and shapes shown in non-standard orientations (e.g. a tilted regular pentagon).

Use a two-way sort with the criteria 'all sides equal?' and 'all angles equal?', giving four groups: 'equal sides but not equal angles', 'equal angles but not equal sides', 'both equal', and 'neither equal'. Place the rhombus, oblong rectangle, square and regular/irregular pentagons.
For each shape, apply a two-column check: sides equal? (tick/cross) | angles equal? (tick/cross), and only call it regular when both columns tick.
Deliberately include an odd-looking regular shape and a tidy-looking irregular shape so that appearance is decoupled from the definition.
activities.title: Sorting with regular/irregular criteria

feedback: If only one counterexample is produced: 'You have the sides-only case — now make an angles-only case (a long rectangle) to show you can fail either condition.'
If the square/rhombus contrast is explained by sides alone: 'Both do have four equal sides. The difference is the angles: the square's four angles are equal, the rhombus's are not.'
Confirm: 'You produced a shape that passes each test separately and explained the square as the one that passes both — that is the full definition in use.'
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to construct counterexamples (equal sides only; equal angles only) shows the learner holds and can apply the full two-part definition, not just recite it.
learnerActions: Draw a shape with all equal sides that is NOT regular (e.g. a rhombus), and label why: equal sides, unequal angles.
Draw a shape with all equal angles that is NOT regular (e.g. an oblong rectangle), and label why: equal angles, unequal sides.
Explain in words why a square is regular but a rhombus is not, even though both have four equal sides.
State the rule by completing: 'a regular polygon has equal ___ and equal ___', then use it to classify a new shape not seen before.
activities.title: Produce a shape that passes one test but fails the other

feedback: If a verdict is given after one condition: 'Before deciding, say what the angles do. Only then can you call it regular or irregular.'
On everyday-language slips: 'Neat or odd-looking does not decide it — a tilted regular pentagon looks unusual but is regular; a tidy oblong is irregular.'
activities.intendedInsight: Verbalising both checks — and resisting a verdict until the second condition is examined — can make the single-criterion habit visible and correctable through talk.
learnerActions: Take the role of, or respond to, a 'shape inspector' who accepts 'regular' only after BOTH conditions are confirmed.
When the learner offers 'the sides are equal', the inspector presses: 'The sides are equal — but what about the angles?' before any verdict is reached.
Talk through the rhombus and the rectangle, each time naming which single condition passes and which fails.
Separate the everyday sense ('regular' = ordinary/tidy) from the mathematical sense by discussing a deliberately odd-looking regular shape and a tidy-looking irregular one.
activities.title: Shape inspector dialogue: always ask the second question
